candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.935 malware probability. All 20 of the top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, and none offsets them. No single n-gram dominates: contributions range from +0.0064 to +0.0149, so the verdict rests on the combined pattern. Three instruction families recur. (1) SIMD register clearing and shuffling: PXOR MOVUPS (+0.014856, the strongest and also the most frequent at 0.001517), PXOR PXOR (+0.012000), MOVUPS PXOR, LEA PXOR, CALL PXOR, MOVQ PUNPCKLQDQ (+0.008081, frequency 0.000790) and CALL MOVHPS. These suggest heavy 128-bit data manipulation, as in hashing or large-state initialization. (2) Rotate and shift arithmetic: ROL MOVZX, MOVZX ROL, ROL ADD, ADD ROR and SHL NEG. These are typical of hash and cipher round functions and bit mixing. (3) Mixed floating-point and integer work: FSTP MOV, MOV FLD, CVTSI2SD PXOR, ADD MOVQ and SUB CMOVG. Combining integer-to-double conversion, x87 and SSE operations, and branchless selects with rotates and SIMD is consistent with a compute-heavy mining kernel, such as a CPU-oriented proof-of-work algorithm. The remaining n-grams (SUB POP, LEA POP, SAR JNZ) look like generic prologue, epilogue or loop code and add little on their own. The evidence has limits. The mnemonics are also common in ordinary compiler-generated math, compression or multimedia code. No function names, API calls or strings were provided, so the classification rests on instruction-level statistical signals and the model's probability. The consistent crypto-style pattern and the high model probability justify high confidence, though not certainty.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Top contributor and relatively frequent. Zeroing an XMM register and then storing or loading 128-bit data is common when initializing large state buffers, as in hash or PoW scratchpads. Compilers also emit it for generic memory clearing, so it is suggestive only.

x87 floating-point store followed by an integer move. This points to mixed floating-point and integer computation, which is unusual in ordinary code and is seen in FP-based mining or VM-style workloads. Very low frequency, but a high SHAP weight.
Loading data into the x87 FPU right after an integer move. Consistent with the floating-point hybrid computation indicated by FSTP MOV.
Consecutive register-clearing or XOR operations on SIMD registers. Typical of vectorized XOR mixing in hash and cipher code, or of unrolled initialization.
Integer addition followed by a transfer between general-purpose and XMM registers. Fits mixing scalar arithmetic with SIMD state, as in mining inner loops.
Bit-shift followed by negation, used for masks and bit manipulation. Rare, but compatible with hash or PRNG-style bit twiddling.
Subtract plus conditional move gives a branchless compare-and-select. Common in constant-time or performance-tuned arithmetic kernels, and moderately supportive.
Rotate followed by zero-extending byte or word load. Resembles the rotate-and-extract steps of hash and cipher rounds.
Addition feeding a right rotate, the add-rotate-xor structure found in hash functions and stream ciphers.
Looks like stack or epilogue handling. Not specific to mining, and its positive SHAP likely reflects the surrounding code structure.
Address computation followed by a register restore, a generic function-boundary pattern. Weak standalone evidence, but the model associates it with this sample.
Rotate then add, another rotate-arithmetic combination typical of cryptographic or hashing round functions.
Integer-to-double conversion followed by a SIMD register clear. Indicates integer-to-floating-point pipelines, consistent with CPU-oriented PoW algorithms that mix FP and integer operations.
Builds a 128-bit vector from two 64-bit values. Fairly frequent, and consistent with SIMD packing of 64-bit state in hashing code.
A call followed by a high-half packed-single move shows SIMD data handling around call boundaries. Mildly supportive of vectorized processing in called routines.
Reverse ordering of ROL MOVZX. Zero-extended byte values feeding rotates fits byte-wise hash or cipher processing, and the pair reinforces that signal.
SIMD XOR or zeroing immediately after a call. This indicates vector-heavy code near call sites, but is not conclusive alone.
Address calculation followed by SIMD XOR or zeroing, consistent with preparing and clearing buffers in vectorized loops.
Unaligned vector load followed by XOR. This is the basic pattern of XOR-based mixing over memory blocks and adds to the PXOR/MOVUPS cluster.
Arithmetic shift followed by a conditional branch, a generic bit-test or loop-control pattern. Weak on its own, but it adds to the cumulative bit-manipulation evidence.
